title: What I Learned at Stanford in 29 Minutes on Power & Influence
summary: Part 3 of Cherie's 'what I learned at Stanford GSB' series covers three soft-skill frameworks: the SBI (situation, behavior, impact) feedback model from the Interpersonal Dynamics 'Touchy Feely' course, power mapping from Jeffrey Pfeffer's Paths to Power class, and the SCQA executive communication structure from Matt Abrahams' strategic comms class. Each is illustrated with corporate case studies (Microsoft, Adobe, Sheryl Sandberg vs. Carol Bartz, Amazon) and a mini exercise, with the central message that being excellent without influence and clear communication is a silent career killer.

ideas.idea: The most valuable things from a $250,000 Stanford MBA were the invisible soft skills, the mental operating systems for building trust and influence, not the hard frameworks and case studies.
ideas.detail: Cherie frames the episode around three such frameworks she applies daily in building Tiger Sisters and in personal relationships.

ideas.idea: Stanford's 'Touchy Feely' (Interpersonal Dynamics) course teaches feedback through a 12-person T-group that sits for three hours with no curriculum until conflict naturally arises and is worked through.
ideas.detail: The class is highly competitive to get into, crying is a rite of passage, it is also embedded in Netflix's culture deck, and Jean's ex broke no-contact to say it changed his life.

ideas.idea: Give feedback with SBI: name the situation (when and where), the observable behavior with no judgment, and the impact on you.
ideas.detail: Feedback must be grounded in a specific observation no one can contest; example: 'in yesterday's client pitch, you interrupted me while I was presenting our strategy, and I felt undermined in front of the client.'

ideas.idea: Feedback fails when people jump straight to impact ('you made me feel bad') without the situation and behavior; say 'I felt X when Y happened' instead of 'you made me feel.'
ideas.detail: The small change in syntax and ordering defuses defensiveness and makes the conversation feel conversational rather than confrontational.

ideas.idea: Never assume another person's intent, only describe the impact of their behavior; assuming intent is 'crossing the net.'
ideas.detail: Intent versus impact is a key distinction from Touchy Feely; you cannot know what is going on in someone else's head.

ideas.idea: SBI works in personal relationships too, including with someone you're dating, though results may vary with immigrant parents.
ideas.detail: Cherie used the 'I felt X when Y' framing with a man she was dating and he thanked her for raising it; she describes herself as being in a 'confrontational phase' where she no longer bottles things up.

ideas.idea: SBI is widely used in corporate performance systems: Microsoft trains all new managers in it and Adobe used it to move away from annual reviews, raising employee satisfaction.
ideas.detail: The hosts cite these as evidence the framework extends beyond Stanford into real management practice.

ideas.idea: Flip SBI to ask for feedback: don't wait for feedback, design for it.
ideas.detail: Example: 'When I shared the product plan in the meeting, what stood out about how I presented it, and what was the impact on the team's decision making?'

ideas.idea: Success isn't only about merit; it's about influence, visibility and alliances, and if you don't understand power you lose to people who do.
ideas.detail: From Jeffrey Pfeffer's Paths to Power class: power is not title, it is who controls resources, influences decisions and pulls strings behind the scenes; Pfeffer's disclaimer is that this is one way to operate, but you should know these moves exist.

ideas.idea: Early in your career you benefit from power dynamics without seeing them; as you get senior, influencing decisions behind the scenes becomes part of your job.
ideas.detail: Jean says she only recognized the power game in the last six years of her career and only started playing it in the last three; Cherie notes juniors aren't privy to how the sausage is made between execs.

ideas.idea: Sheryl Sandberg's career is a model of accumulating influence across sectors rather than titles.
ideas.detail: She learned where power sits as chief of staff at the US Treasury, built a cross-functional web of influence in biz ops at Google reporting to Eric Schmidt, and by the time she met Mark Zuckerberg at a 2007 Christmas party her multi-sector power map was her most valuable asset.

ideas.idea: Power isn't about being right; it's about having enough support and alliances to survive being right.
ideas.detail: Carol Bartz, a highly capable CEO brought in to turn around Yahoo, focused on tactical execution and never built internal allies, so her objectively correct radical moves lacked support and she was fired by phone.

ideas.idea: Map your own power web: pick the five people who will influence your next raise, role or deal, classify each as advocate, neutral or unaware, and connect with one this week.
ideas.detail: Being excellent without visibility is a silent career killer, especially if you're brilliant; those who understand the game won't tell you because it would give away their edge.

ideas.idea: If you can't get to your point in 30 seconds, people tune out; being clear is more powerful than being smart.
ideas.detail: Jean used to think being smart meant long detailed explanations; the hosts note Donald Trump's communication is powerful precisely because he reduces everything to the simplest words, e.g. 'big beautiful bill.'

ideas.idea: Structure any pitch with SCQA: situation, complication, question, answer.
ideas.detail: Example: 'CAC is rising faster than LTV (S); if we don't adjust we'll overspend (C); what do we do (Q); shift 40% of spend to UGC creators (A).' The method comes from Barbara Minto and is taught by Matt Abrahams, who coached Cherie for her TED talk.

ideas.idea: Practice simplifying language deliberately, the way Glenn Kramon's writing class at Stanford opens each session by simplifying ten terms.
ideas.detail: Cherie offers this 'simplify, simplify, simplify' drill as a bonus exercise for clearer communication.

ideas.idea: Amazon uses SCQA in the mock press release inside its six-page product launch memos to state the user pain point and what the product solves.
ideas.detail: The hosts cite this as the corporate case study for the framework.

ideas.idea: Test your pitch by writing it in SCQA, saying it aloud, and reading it to a friend; if they can repeat the idea back in one sentence you've done it right.
ideas.detail: This is the mini exercise for the executive communication framework.
